<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Every \(\delta\)-ULC probability measure \(\mu\) satisfies
    \begin{equation}
        \delta\,\*{Var}_\mu\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n\sim\mu}\left[\sum_{i=1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \left(\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right], \quad \forall f
        \label{eq:intro-weighted-poincare}
    \end{equation}
    Equivalently, the canonical birth-death generator \(\+L\) has spectral gap at least \(\delta\); the spectral gap is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of \(-\+L\) in \(L^2\left(\mu\right)\).
    \label{thm:intro-weighted-poincare}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Suppose that \(\*K_{\*n}\) is positive definite for every \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\). Then
\[
\*{Var}_\mu\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)_{\+I_{\*n}}^{\top} \*K_{\*n}^{-1} \left(\nabla^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)_{\+I_{\*n}}\right], \quad \forall f.
\]
\label{thm:intro-brascamp-lieb}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
Every ULC probability measure \(\mu\) with finite first moments satisfies the weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(1\):
\begin{equation}
    \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i=1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \Psi\left(f\left(\*n\right),\nabla_i^+f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right] \le \+E\left(\log f,f\right), \quad \forall f > 0,
    \label{eq:intro-weighted-wu-inequality}
\end{equation}
where
\[
\Psi\left(u,v\right) := \left(u + v\right) \log\left(u + v\right) - u \log u - v \left(\log u + 1\right),
\]
and \(\+E\) denotes the Dirichlet form associated with \(\+L\). In particular, \(\+L\) satisfies the modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(1\).
\label{thm:intro-wu-mlsi}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
If \(\mu\) satisfies the weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(1\), i.e., \eqref{eq:intro-weighted-wu-inequality} holds, and has finite positive mean \(\*m\), then the following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Poisson domination:} For every \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathbb R^d\),
    \begin{equation}
        \*E_{\*X \sim \mu}\left[e^{\left\langle\boldsymbol{\lambda},\,\*X\right\rangle}\right] \le \exp\left(\sum_{i = 1}^d m_i \left(e^{\lambda_i} - 1\right)\right) = \*E_{\*Z \sim \pi_{\*m}}\left[e^{\left\langle\boldsymbol{\lambda},\,\*Z\right\rangle}\right].
    \label{eq:intro-mgf-comparison}
    \end{equation}

    \item \textbf{Concentration of measure:} For \(\*t \in \mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(t_i > -m_i\) for every \(i \in \left[d\right]\), define the orthant event
    \[
    \+O_{\*t} := \bigcap_{\substack{i \in \left[d\right] \\ t_i > 0}} \left\{X_i - m_i \ge t_i\right\} \cap \bigcap_{\substack{i \in \left[d\right] \\ t_i < 0}} \left\{X_i - m_i \le t_i\right\}.
    \]
    Then
    \begin{equation}
        \*{Pr}_{\mu}\left[\+O_{\*t}\right] \le \exp\left(-\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{t_i^2}{2 m_i} h\left(\frac{t_i}{m_i}\right)\right),
        \label{eq:intro-concentration}
    \end{equation}
    where
    \[  
    h\left(x\right) := 2 \frac{\left(1 + x\right) \log\left(1 + x\right) - x}{x^2}, \quad x \ge -1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Maximum-entropy principle:} For a distribution \(\nu\) on \(\mathbb N^d\), define its Shannon entropy as \(H\left(\nu\right) := -\sum_{\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right)} \nu\left(\*n\right) \log \nu\left(\*n\right)\). Then
    \begin{equation}
        H\left(\pi_{\*m}\right) - H\left(\mu\right) \ge \-{KL}\left(\mu \| \pi_{\*m}\right) \ge 0.
        \label{eq:intro-maximum-entropy}
    \end{equation}
    Here, \(\-{KL}\left(\mu \| \pi_{\*m}\right)\) denotes the relative entropy of \(\mu\) with respect to \(\pi_{\*m}\). Consequently, among all ULC measures with mean \(\*m\), the product Poisson measure \(\pi_{\*m}\) is the unique entropy maximizer.
\end{enumerate}
\label{thm:intro-concentration}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The Markov chain \(P\) is irreducible if, for all \(x, y \in \Omega\), there exists \(t \in \mathbb N\) such that \(P^t\left(x, y\right) > 0\). It is aperiodic if, for every \(x \in \Omega\), \(\gcd\left\{t \in \mathbb N_{> 0} \,:\, P^t\left(x, x\right) > 0\right\} = 1\). It is ergodic if it is both irreducible and aperiodic.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
Let \(P\) be an ergodic Markov chain on a finite state space \(\Omega\). Then \(P\) has a unique stationary distribution \(\mu\), and for every initial distribution \(\nu\) on \(\Omega\), \(\nu P^t \to \mu\) pointwise as \(t \to \infty\).
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let \(P\) be an ergodic Markov chain on a finite state space \(\Omega\) with stationary distribution \(\mu\). For \(\varepsilon \in \left(0, 1\right)\), the \(\varepsilon\)-mixing time of \(P\) is
    \[
    T_{\-{mix}}\left(\varepsilon; P\right) := \max_{x \in \Omega} \min\left\{t \in \mathbb N \,:\, \-{TV}\left(P^t\left(x, \cdot\right), \mu\right) \le \varepsilon\right\}.
    \]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let \(\+L\) be a reversible Markov generator with stationary measure \(\mu\) and Dirichlet form \(\+E\).
    \begin{itemize}
        \item We say that \(\+L\) satisfies a Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\gamma > 0\) if
        \[
        \gamma \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \+E\left(f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+D\left(\+E\right).
        \]
        The optimal constant \(\gamma\) is called the spectral gap of \(\+L\); for an irreducible finite-state chain, it is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of \(-\+L\).
        \item We say that \(\+L\) satisfies a modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\rho > 0\) if
        \[
        \rho \, \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \+E\left(\log f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+A,
        \]
        where \(\+A := \left\{f \in \+D\left(\+E\right) \,:\, f > 0, \, \log f \in \+D\left(\+E\right)\right\}\).
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
Let \(P\) be an ergodic reversible Markov chain on a finite state space \(\Omega\) with at least two states and stationary distribution \(\mu\), and suppose that \(P\) is positive semidefinite on \(L^2\left(\mu\right)\). Set \(\mu_{\min} := \min_{x \in \Omega} \mu\left(x\right)\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon \in \left(0, 1 / 2\right)\), the following statements hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(P\) satisfies a Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\gamma\), then
        \[
        T_{\-{mix}}\left(\varepsilon; P\right) \le \left\lceil\frac{1}{\gamma} \left(\log\frac{1}{2 \varepsilon} + \frac{1}{2} \log \frac{1}{\mu_{\min}}\right)\right\rceil.
        \]
        \item If \(P\) satisfies a modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\rho\), then
        \[
        T_{\-{mix}}\left(\varepsilon; P\right) \le \left\lceil\frac{1}{\rho} \left(\log\frac{1}{2 \varepsilon^2} + \log\log \frac{1}{\mu_{\min}}\right)\right\rceil.
        \]
    \end{itemize}
    \label{thm:functional-inequality-mixing}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
For a reversible kernel, lazification---replacing \(P\) with \(\bar P := \left(I + P\right) / 2\)---ensures positive semidefiniteness.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
The carr\'e du champ and iterated carr\'e du champ operators associated with \(\+L\) are
    \[
    \Gamma\left(f, g\right) := \frac{1}{2} \left[\+L\left(fg\right) - f \+L g - g \+L f\right], \qquad \Gamma_2\left(f, g\right) := \frac{1}{2} \left[\+L\Gamma\left(f, g\right) - \Gamma\left(f, \+L g\right) - \Gamma\left(g, \+L f\right)\right].
    \]
    \label{def:carre-du-champ-operators}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:integrated-bakry-emery-criterion}
    Let \(\+L\) be the generator of an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space \(\Omega\), reversible with respect to \(\mu\). For \(\delta > 0\), the following statements are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The generator \(\+L\) satisfies the Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\delta\).
        \item For every \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb R\),
        \[
        \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma_2\left(f, f\right)\right] \ge \delta \, \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma\left(f, f\right)\right].
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
    Consequently, the pointwise condition \(\-{CD}\left(\delta, \infty\right)\) implies the Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\delta\).
    \label{thm:integrated-bakry-emery}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let \(0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 \le \cdots \le \lambda_{\left|\Omega\right| - 1}\) be the eigenvalues of \(-\+L\), counted with multiplicity. Expanding a mean-zero function \(f\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis and using \eqref{eq:integrated-carre-du-champ-identities} shows that the Poincar\'e\xspace inequality is equivalent to \(\lambda_k \ge \delta\) for every \(k \ge 1\). The integrated Bakry--\'Emery\xspace inequality is equivalent to \(\lambda_k^2 \ge \delta \lambda_k\) for every \(k \ge 1\), which is the same condition.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
Consider the birth-death generator \(\+L\) defined in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator}, and set \(a\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\) for \(\*n \in \mathbb N^d\). Then the identity below holds for every \(f, g \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\):
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma_2\left(f, g\right)\right] =& \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right] \\
        &+ \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} \left(\frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)^2} - \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)}\right) \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right] \\
        &+ \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    \label{thm:integrated-gamma-2-form}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The identity in \Cref{thm:integrated-gamma-2-form} is a discrete analogue of the Bochner formula for the Langevin generator \(\+L = \Delta - \nabla V \cdot \nabla\) on \(\mathbb R^d\):
    \[
    \Gamma_2\left(f, g\right) = \left\langle\nabla^2 f,\,\nabla^2 g\right\rangle_{\-{HS}} + \nabla f^{\top} \nabla^2 V \nabla g.
    \]
    The first term is a second-order energy, which is non-negative when \(f = g\). The second term is a first-order form determined by the local curvature of the potential \(V = -\log \mu\). Likewise, the first line of the identity in \Cref{thm:integrated-gamma-2-form} is a weighted discrete Hessian energy. The remaining two lines define a first-order form whose coefficients compare neighboring ratios of \(a\left(\*n\right) = \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\), thereby serving as a discrete analogue of the curvature matrix \(\nabla^2 V\).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since \(f, g \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) and the birth-death graph is locally finite, \(\+L f\), \(\+L g\), and every summand appearing below are finitely supported. Hence all expectations are finite, and every change of variables is justified directly.

    For \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), define the ratios
    \[
    r_i\left(\*n\right) := \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)}, \qquad r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) := \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)}.
    \]
    These quantities are extended by zero outside the support. Reversibility of \(\+L\) and the definition of \(\Gamma_2\) imply
    \[
    \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma_2\left(f, g\right)\right] = -\frac{1}{2} \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma\left(f, \+L g\right) + \Gamma\left(g, \+L f\right)\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\+L f \, \+L g\right].
    \]
    Then the required discrete Bochner formula is
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E_{\mu}\left[\+L f \, \+L g\right]
        =& \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right] + \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right] \\
        &+ \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} \left(r_i\left(\*n\right) r_j\left(\*n\right) - r_{ij}\left(\*n\right)\right) \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    
    To verify this identity, write
    \[
    u_i\left(\*n\right) := \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right), \qquad v_j\left(\*n\right) := \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right).
    \]
    Note that \(r_i\left(\*n\right)\) is exactly the birth rate \(b_i\left(\*n\right)\) in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator}. The generator can then be written entirely in terms of forward differences as
    \[
    \+L f\left(\*n\right) = \sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) - \sum_{\substack{i \in \left[d\right] \\ n_i > 0}} n_i u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right),
    \]
    and analogously for \(g\). In the sums below, a predecessor term is understood to vanish when the corresponding coordinate is zero. We use the following identities:
    \[
    \mu\left(\*n\right) n_i = \mu\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) r_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right), \qquad r_i\left(\*n\right) r_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) = r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) = r_j\left(\*n\right) r_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right).
    \]

    Expand the product \(\+L f \, \+L g\) into four terms:
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \+L f\left(\*n\right) \+L g\left(\*n\right) =& \underbrace{\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) r_j\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)}_{\text{birth--birth}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} n_i n_j u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) v_j\left(\*n - \*e_j\right)}_{\text{death--death}} \\
        &- \underbrace{\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) n_j u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n - \*e_j\right) - \sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} n_i r_j\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)}_{\text{birth--death}}.
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    The birth--birth product in \(\*E_{\mu}\left[\+L f \, \+L g\right]\) is
    \[
    \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) r_j\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \]
    For the death--death product, first consider \(i \ne j\). Shifting \(\*n\) to \(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\) yields
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{\substack{i, j \in \left[d\right] \\ i \ne j}} n_i n_j u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) v_j\left(\*n - \*e_j\right)\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{\substack{i, j \in \left[d\right] \\ i \ne j}} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right) v_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)\right].
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    On the diagonal, the decomposition \(n_i^2 = n_i \left(n_i - 1\right) + n_i\), followed by shifts by \(2\*e_i\) and \(\*e_i\), respectively, gives
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} n_i^2 u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) v_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right)\right] =& \, \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} r_{ii}\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) v_i\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)\right] \\
        &+ \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_i\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    For the first birth--death product, shifting \(\*n\) to \(\*n + \*e_j\) and using detailed balance gives
    \[
    \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) n_j u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n - \*e_j\right)\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \]
    Similarly, shifting the second birth--death product by \(\*e_i\) gives
    \[
    \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} n_i r_j\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)\right].
    \]
    Combining these four products gives
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E_{\mu}\left[\+L f \, \+L g\right]
        =& \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) \left(u_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right) v_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) - u_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right) v_j\left(\*n\right) - u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)\right)\right] \\
        &+ \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) r_j\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right] + \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} r_i\left(\*n\right) u_i\left(\*n\right) v_i\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Finally,
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        u_i\left(\*n + \*e_j\right) - u_i\left(\*n\right) &= \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ f\left(\*n\right), \\
        v_j\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) - v_j\left(\*n\right) &= \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right),
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    and the elementary identity \(U'V' - U'V - UV' = \left(U' - U\right)\left(V' - V\right) - UV\) transforms the first line into
    \[
    \*E_{\mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} r_{ij}\left(\*n\right) \left(\nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right) - u_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right)\right].
    \]
    Substituting the definitions of \(r_i\), \(r_{ij}\), \(u_i\), \(v_j\) yields the claimed formula.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\) with downward closed support, and define \(a\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\) for \(\*n \in \mathbb N^d\). We say that \(\mu\) is ultra-log-concave with parameter \(\delta > 0\), or \(\delta\)-ULC, if the following inequality holds for every \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\):
    \begin{equation}
        \left(1 - \frac{a\left(\*n\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)}\right)_{i, j \in \+I_{\*n}} + \left(1 - \delta\right) \operatorname{diag} \left(\frac{a\left(\*n\right)}{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}\right)_{i \in \+I_{\*n}} \succeq \*O.
        \label{eq:ulc-condition}
    \end{equation}
    Here, \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n + \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\) denotes the set of coordinates along which a birth transition is possible from \(\*n\). In particular, we say \(\mu\) is ultra-log-concave, or ULC, if it is \(1\)-ULC.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
Every \(\delta\)-ULC probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb N^d\) satisfies the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\delta\):
    \[
    \delta \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right], \quad \forall f \in \+D\left(\+E\right).
    \]
    Equivalently, the birth-death generator \(\+L\) defined in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator} has spectral gap at least \(\delta\).
    \label{thm:ulc-poincare-inequality}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
For measures supported on subsets of the hypercube \(\left\{0, 1\right\}^d\), the \(\delta\)-ULC condition and the resulting Poincar\'e\xspace inequality have previously appeared in \cite[Theorem~1.9]{CCCYZ25} and \cite[Theorem~1.2]{GJMPPS26}. An infinite-dimensional counterpart for point processes, whose configuration space may be viewed as an infinite-dimensional hypercube, appeared earlier in \cite[Theorem~3.4]{KKO13}. For a more detailed discussion of the connection between Glauber dynamics for point processes and birth-death chains for probability measures on \(\mathbb N^d\), see \Cref{sec:point-processes}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For completeness, we make the passage to infinite support explicit. For \(N \in \mathbb N\), let
    \[
    S_N := \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right) \cap \left\{\*n \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \left\|\*n\right\|_{\infty} \le N\right\}, \qquad \mu_N\left(\*n\right) := \frac{\mu\left(\*n\right)}{\mu\left(S_N\right)}, \quad \*n \in S_N.
    \]
    The set \(S_N\) is finite and downward closed. The ULC matrix for \(\mu_N\) is obtained from the ULC matrix for \(\mu\) by restricting to the active coordinates in \(S_N\) and, when a second step exits the box, adding a non-negative diagonal matrix. Hence \(\mu_N\) is also \(\delta\)-ULC. The finite-state integrated Bakry--\'Emery\xspace criterion therefore gives
    \[
    \delta \, \*{Var}_{\mu_N}\left[f\right] \le \+E_N\left(f, f\right)
    \]
    for every function on \(S_N\). If \(f \in \+D\left(\+E\right)\), then \(\*{Var}_{\mu_N}\left[f\right] \to \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right]\) and \(\+E_N\left(f, f\right) \to \+E\left(f, f\right)\) as \(N \to \infty\). Passing to the limit proves the claimed inequality on \(\+D\left(\+E\right)\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
In one dimension, the \(\delta\)-ULC condition becomes
    \[
    1 - \frac{a\left(n\right) a\left(n + 2\right)}{a \left(n + 1\right)^2} + \left(1 - \delta\right) \frac{a\left(n\right)}{a\left(n + 1\right)} \ge 0, \quad \forall n \,:\, n + 1 \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
    If equality holds for every \(n\) such that \(n + 1 \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), then a direct computation yields the following classification:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(\delta \in \left(0, 1\right)\), then \(\mu\) is a negative binomial distribution \(\-{NB}\left(r, \delta\right)\) for some \(r > 0\).
        \item If \(\delta = 1\), then \(\mu\) is a Poisson distribution \(\-{Pois}\left(\lambda\right)\) for some \(\lambda > 0\).
        \item If \(\delta > 1\), then \(\mu\) is a binomial distribution \(\-{Bin}\left(N, 1 - 1 / \delta\right)\) for some \(N \in \mathbb N_{> 0}\).
    \end{itemize}
    Moreover, \(\delta\) is the optimal constant in the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality for \(\mu\); equivalently, the birth-death generator \(\+L\) defined in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator} has spectral gap \(\delta\). The centered identity function \(f\left(n\right) := n - \!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\) is an eigenfunction of \(-\+L\) with eigenvalue \(\delta\).
    \label{ex:ulc-exact-1d}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
In one dimension, the ULC condition becomes
    \[
    1 - \frac{a\left(n\right) a\left(n + 2\right)}{a \left(n + 1\right)^2} \ge 0, \quad \forall n \,:\, n + 1 \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
    Equivalently, the sequence \(a\left(n\right) = n! \mu\left(n\right)\) is log-concave. This is precisely the classical notion of an ultra-log-concave measure, an important class of discrete probability measures; see \cite[Section~1]{AMM21} for further discussion. By \Cref{thm:ulc-poincare-inequality}, every ULC measure on \(\mathbb N\) satisfies the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{n \sim \mu}\left[\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \mu\left(n + 1\right)}{\mu\left(n\right)} \left(\nabla^+ f\left(n\right)\right)^2\right], \quad \forall f \in \+D\left(\+E\right).
    \]
    Moreover, ultra-log-concavity of \(\mu\) implies that the ratios
    \[
    \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \mu\left(n + 1\right)}{\mu\left(n\right)} = \frac{a\left(n + 1\right)}{a\left(n\right)}, \quad n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right),
    \]
    are non-increasing in \(n\). In particular, they are bounded above by \(\mu\left(1\right) / \mu\left(0\right)\). Consequently, the weighted inequality above yields the classical unweighted discrete Poincar\'e\xspace inequality
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \frac{\mu\left(1\right)}{\mu\left(0\right)} \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ f\right)^2\right], \quad \forall f \in \+D\left(\+E\right).
    \]
    This recovers \cite[Theorem~1.5]{Joh17}. The constant \(\mu\left(1\right)/\mu\left(0\right)\), however, is not optimal for the class of ULC measures: it can be improved to \(\!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\); see \cite[Corollary~2.4]{DJ13}.
    \label{ex:one-dim-ulc-poincare}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
Let \(\mu := \bigotimes_{i = 1}^d \mu_i\) be a product measure on \(\mathbb N^d\). Then \(\mu\) is \(\delta\)-ULC if and only if each factor \(\mu_i\) is \(\delta\)-ULC. The spectral gap of the birth-death generator \(\+L\) defined in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator} is exactly the minimum of the spectral gaps of the one-dimensional generators.
    \label{ex:ulc-product-measure}
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
Fix \(b_{\-{long}}, b_{\-{short}} > 0\) and consider two queues with \(M/M/\infty\)-type service: at state \(\*n \in \mathbb N^2\), customers depart queue \(i\) at rate \(n_i\). Arrivals join the longer queue at rate \(b_{\-{long}}\) and the shorter queue at rate \(b_{\-{short}}\); when the queues are tied, each receives arrivals at rate \(b_{\-{long}}\). The queue-length vector therefore evolves as a birth-death chain on \(\mathbb N^2\), reversible with respect to
    \[
    \mu\left(\*n\right) \propto \frac{1}{\*n!} b_{\-{long}}^{\max\left\{n_1, n_2\right\}} b_{\-{short}}^{\min\left\{n_1, n_2\right\}}, \quad \*n \in \mathbb N^2.
    \]
    Indeed, the ratio \(\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) / \mu\left(\*n\right)\) equals \(b_{\-{long}}\) when \(n_i \ge n_{3 - i}\) and \(b_{\-{short}}\) otherwise, exactly reproducing the prescribed birth rates.

    Write \(\Delta b := b_{\-{long}} - b_{\-{short}}\), and let \(\*M_{\delta}\left(\*n\right)\) denote the matrix on the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:ulc-condition}. For \(n_1 \ge n_2\), a direct computation yields
    \[
    \*M_{\delta}\left(\*n\right) = \begin{cases}
        \left(1 - \delta\right) \operatorname{diag}\left(b_{\-{long}}^{-1}, b_{\-{short}}^{-1}\right), & n_1 \ge n_2 + 2, \\
        \operatorname{diag}\left(b_{\-{long}}^{-1} \left(1 - \delta\right), b_{\-{short}}^{-1} \left(1 - \delta - \Delta b\right)\right), & n_1 = n_2 + 1, \\
        b_{\-{long}}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 - \delta & \Delta b \\ \Delta b & 1 - \delta \end{pmatrix}, & n_1 = n_2.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    For \(n_2 > n_1\), the matrix is obtained by interchanging the two coordinates. These matrices are positive semidefinite if and only if \(\delta \le 1 - \left|\Delta b\right|\). Hence a positive ULC parameter exists precisely when \(\left|\Delta b\right| < 1\). In that case, \(\mu\) is \(\left(1 - \left|\Delta b\right|\right)\)-ULC, and the queueing process has spectral gap at least \(1 - \left|\Delta b\right|\).
    \label{ex:two-queue-model}
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\) with downward closed support, and let \(\*K_{\*n}\) be the local curvature matrix defined in \eqref{eq:local-curvature-matrix}. Suppose that \(\*K_{\*n} \succ \*O\) for every \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\). Then
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}\right], \quad \forall f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right),
    \]
    where \(\left(\cdot\right)_{\+I_{\*n}}\) denotes the restriction to the coordinates in \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n + \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\). The integrand on the right-hand side is evaluated using the corresponding local quantities; that is, \(\*K = \*K_{\*n}\), \(\+I = \+I_{\*n}\), and \(\nabla^+ f = \nabla^+ f\left(\*n\right)\).
    \label{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The inequality extends by continuity to the completion of \(\+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) with respect to the norm
    \[
    \left\|f\right\|_{\-{BL}}^2 := \left\|f\right\|_{L^2\left(\mu\right)}^2 + \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}\right].
    \]
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
If \(\mu\) is \(\delta\)-ULC, then \eqref{eq:ulc-curvature-lower-bound} implies
    \[
    \*K_{\*n}^{-1} \preceq \frac{1}{\delta} \operatorname{diag} \left(\frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)}\right)_{i \in \+I_{\*n}}, \quad \forall \*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
    Hence \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb} recovers the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality in \Cref{thm:ulc-poincare-inequality}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
First suppose that \(\mu\) is finitely supported and replace \(f\) by \(f - \*E_{\mu}\left[f\right]\).
    
    Let \(g := \left(-\+L\right)^{\dagger} f\), where \(\+L\) is the birth-death generator defined in \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator}, and \(\left(-\+L\right)^{\dagger}\) is its Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. Then \(g\) is the unique solution to the Poisson equation \(-\+L g = f\) with \(\*E_{\mu}\left[g\right] = 0\).

    By reversibility of \(\+L\) and \eqref{eq:birth-death-dirichlet-form},
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[f^2\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[f \, \left(-\+L\right) g\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma\left(f, g\right)\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right].
    \]
    For \(i \in \+I_{\*n}\), write \(u_i\left(\*n\right) := \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\) and \(v_i\left(\*n\right) := \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right)\). Then the above expression becomes
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \+I_{\*n}} u_i\left(\*n\right) v_i\left(\*n\right)\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\*u^{\top} \*v\right].
    \]
    Since \(\*K_{\*n} \succ \*O\) for every \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
            \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] &= \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\*K^{-1 / 2} \*u\right)^{\top} \left(\*K^{1 / 2} \*v\right)\right] \\
            &\le \*E_{\mu}\left[\left\|\*K^{-1 / 2} \*u\right\|_2^2\right]^{1 / 2} \*E_{\mu}\left[\left\|\*K^{1 / 2} \*v\right\|_2^2\right]^{1 / 2} \\
            &= \*E_{\mu}\left[\*u^{\top} \*K^{-1} \*u\right]^{1 / 2} \*E_{\mu}\left[\*v^{\top} \*K \*v\right]^{1 / 2}.
        \end{aligned}
        \label{eq:discrete-brascamp-lieb-cauchy-schwarz}
    \end{equation}

    On the other hand,
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[f^2\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\+L g\right)^2\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\Gamma_2\left(g, g\right)\right].
    \]
    By the discrete Bochner formula in \Cref{thm:integrated-gamma-2-form},
    \begin{align*}
        \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] &= \, \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] + \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \left[d\right]} \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] \\
        &\phantom{={}} + \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \left[d\right]} \left(\frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)^2} - \frac{a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n\right)}\right) \nabla_i^+ g\left(\*n\right) \nabla_j^+ g\left(\*n\right)\right] \\
        &\ge \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i, j \in \+I_{\*n}} \left(1 - \frac{a\left(\*n\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)}\right) v_i\left(\*n\right) v_j\left(\*n\right)\right] + \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \+I_{\*n}} \frac{a\left(\*n\right)}{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)} v_i\left(\*n\right)^2\right] \\
        &= \*E_{\mu}\left[\*v^{\top} \*K \*v\right].
    \end{align*}
    Together with \eqref{eq:discrete-brascamp-lieb-cauchy-schwarz}, this gives
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\mu}\left[\*u^{\top} \*K^{-1} \*u\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^+ f\right)_{\+I}\right].
    \]

    To pass to an arbitrary downward closed support, fix \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) and use the coordinate-box restrictions \(S_N\) and conditional measures \(\mu_N\) introduced in the proof of \Cref{thm:ulc-poincare-inequality}. The local curvature matrix for \(\mu_N\) is obtained by restricting \(\*K_{\*n}\) to the active coordinates in \(S_N\) and adding non-negative diagonal entries when a second step exits the box; it is therefore positive definite. Apply the finite-state inequality to \(f|_{S_N}\). For all sufficiently large \(N\), every state at which \(\nabla^+ f\) is nonzero lies away from the boundary of the box, so its local curvature matrix agrees with \(\*K_{\*n}\). Letting \(N \to \infty\) proves the inequality for \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
In the same setting as \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb}, we have
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \preceq \*E_{\mu}\left[P_{\+I}^{\top}\*K^{-1} P_{\+I}\right],
    \]
    where \(P_{\+I_{\*n}}\) is the projection onto the active coordinates \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n + \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\). In other words, \(P_{\+I_{\*n}}^{\top}\*K_{\*n}^{-1} P_{\+I_{\*n}}\) is simply \(\*K_{\*n}^{-1}\) zero-padded to \(\mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\).
    \label{cor:discrete-brascamp-lieb-cov-bound}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For any \(\*v \ne \*0\), consider the linear test function \(\ell_{\*v}\left(\*n\right) := \*v^{\top} \*n\). \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb} gives
    \[
    \*v^{\top} \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \*v = \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[\ell_{\*v}\right] \le \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^+ \ell_{\*v}\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^+ \ell_{\*v}\right)_{\+I}\right] = \*E_{\mu}\left[\*v_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \*v_{\+I}\right] = \*v^{\top} \*E_{\mu}\left[P_{\+I}^{\top}\*K^{-1} P_{\+I}\right] \*v.
    \]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb Z^d\) with upward closed support. For each \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), define the local curvature matrix
    \[
    \*K_{\*n} := \left(1 - \frac{\mu\left(\*n\right) \mu\left(\*n - \*e_i - \*e_j\right)}{\mu\left(\*n - \*e_i\right) \mu\left(\*n - \*e_j\right)}\right)_{i, j \in \+I_{\*n}},
    \]
    where \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n - \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\). Suppose that \(\*K_{\*n} \succ \*O\) for every \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\). Then
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^- f\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^- f\right)_{\+I}\right], \quad \forall f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right),
    \]
    where \(\left(\cdot\right)_{\+I_{\*n}}\) denotes the restriction to the coordinates in \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n - \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\). The integrand on the right-hand side is evaluated using the corresponding local quantities; that is, \(\*K = \*K_{\*n}\), \(\+I = \+I_{\*n}\), and \(\nabla^- f = \nabla^- f\left(\*n\right)\).
    \label{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb-unit-birth}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The inequality extends by continuity to the completion of \(\+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) with respect to the norm
    \[
    \left\|f\right\|_{\-{BL}, -}^2 := \left\|f\right\|_{L^2\left(\mu\right)}^2 + \*E_{\mu}\left[\left(\nabla^- f\right)_{\+I}^{\top} \*K^{-1} \left(\nabla^- f\right)_{\+I}\right].
    \]
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Under the \(c\)-log-concavity condition,
    \[
    \*K_{\*n}^{-1} \preceq \frac{1}{c} \, \operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{\mu\left(\*n - \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)}\right)_{i \in \+I_{\*n}}, \quad \forall \*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
    Consequently, \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb-unit-birth} recovers the Poincar\'e\xspace inequality proved in \cite{Joh17}. Indeed,
    \[
    \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \frac{1}{c} \*E_{\mu}\left[\sum_{i \in \+I_{\*n}} \frac{\mu\left(\*n - \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^- f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] = \frac{1}{c} \*E_{\mu}\left[\left\|\nabla^+ f\right\|_2^2\right], \quad \forall f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right).
    \]
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
In the same setting as \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb-unit-birth}, we have
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \preceq \*E_{\mu}\left[P_{\+I}^{\top}\*K^{-1} P_{\+I}\right],
    \]
    where \(P_{\+I_{\*n}}\) is the projection onto the active coordinates \(\+I_{\*n} := \left\{i \in \left[d\right] \,:\, \*n - \*e_i \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right\}\). In other words, \(P_{\+I_{\*n}}^{\top}\*K_{\*n}^{-1} P_{\+I_{\*n}}\) is simply \(\*K_{\*n}^{-1}\) zero-padded to \(\mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\).
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
Let \(G\) be \(\Delta\)-regular, let \(\*A_G\) be its adjacency matrix, and set \(\lambda^{\star} := -\lambda_{\min}\left(\*A_G\right)\). Suppose that
    \[
    1 + \lambda^{-1} \ge \lambda^{\star}.
    \]
    Then
    \[
    V_G\left(\lambda\right) \le \frac{\lambda}{1 + \left(\Delta + 1\right) \lambda}.
    \]
    \label{thm:hardcore-cardinality-variance}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
A related variance bound follows from the spectral-independence consequences of \(\delta\)-ULC. In particular, for \(\delta \in \left(0, 1\right)\), the stronger low-fugacity condition
    \[
    1 + \left(1 - \delta\right) \lambda^{-1} > \lambda^{\star}
    \]
    implies that \(\mu_{G, \lambda}\) is \(\delta\)-ULC; see \cite[Section~5.2]{CCCYZ25}. By \Cref{cor:ulc-cov-bound}, it is therefore \(1 / \delta\)-spectrally independent:
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\mu_{G, \lambda}\right) \preceq \frac{1}{\delta} \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\mu_{G, \lambda}\right)\right),
    \]
    and hence
    \[
    V_G\left(\lambda\right) \le \frac{1}{\delta} \alpha_G\left(\lambda\right).
    \]
    At the boundary \(1 + \lambda^{-1} = \lambda^{\star}\), no positive \(\delta\) satisfies the stronger condition, so this estimate degenerates. In contrast, the bound in \Cref{thm:hardcore-cardinality-variance} remains finite at the boundary because it retains the full local curvature matrix and evaluates its inverse in the direction \(\*1_V\).
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For \(I \in \+I\left(G\right)\), let \(N_G\left(I\right)\) be the open neighborhood of \(I\), and define the set of unblocked vertices by
    \[
    V_I := V \setminus \left(I \cup N_G\left(I\right)\right).
    \]
    These vertices are precisely the active birth coordinates at \(I\). Substituting the hardcore weights into \eqref{eq:local-curvature-matrix} gives
    \begin{equation}
        \*K_I = \*A_{G\left[V_I\right]} + \left(1 + \lambda^{-1}\right) \*I_{V_I},
        \label{eq:hardcore-local-curvature}
    \end{equation}
    where \(\*A_{G\left[V_I\right]}\) is the adjacency matrix of the subgraph induced by \(V_I\).

    Set \(s := 1 + \lambda^{-1}\), and first suppose that \(s > \lambda^{\star}\). The curvature matrix at the empty independent set is
    \[
    \*K_{\varnothing} = \*A_G + s \*I_V \succ \*O.
    \]
    By \eqref{eq:hardcore-local-curvature}, each \(\*K_I\) is a principal submatrix of \(\*K_{\varnothing}\) and is therefore positive definite. Applying \Cref{thm:discrete-brascamp-lieb} to the cardinality function \(f\left(I\right) := \left|I\right|\), for which \(\nabla_v^+ f\left(I\right) = 1\) whenever \(v \in V_I\), gives
    \[
    \*{Var}\left[\left|I\right|\right] \le \*E\left[\*1_{V_I}^{\top} \*K_I^{-1} \*1_{V_I}\right],
    \]
    where \(\*1_{V_I}\) denotes the all-ones vector indexed by \(V_I\).

    Fix \(I \in \+I\left(G\right)\), and extend vectors indexed by \(V_I\) by zero outside \(V_I\). The variational representation of an inverse quadratic form gives
    \[
    \*1_{V_I}^{\top} \*K_I^{-1} \*1_{V_I} = \sup_{\*z \in \mathbb{R}^{V_I}} \left(2 \*1_{V_I}^{\top} \*z - \*z^{\top} \*K_I \*z\right) \le \sup_{\*z \in \mathbb{R}^V} \left(2 \*1_V^{\top} \*z - \*z^{\top} \*K_{\varnothing} \*z\right) = \*1_V^{\top} \*K_{\varnothing}^{-1} \*1_V.
    \]
    Since \(G\) is \(\Delta\)-regular,
    \[
    \*K_{\varnothing} \*1_V = \left(\Delta + s\right) \*1_V,
    \]
    so
    \[
    \*1_V^{\top} \*K_{\varnothing}^{-1} \*1_V = \frac{\left|V\right|}{\Delta + s} = \frac{\left|V\right| \lambda}{1 + \left(\Delta + 1\right) \lambda}.
    \]
    Combining the preceding inequalities and dividing by \(\left|V\right|\) proves the claim when \(s > \lambda^{\star}\).

    If \(s = \lambda^{\star}\), choose \(\lambda_k \to \lambda^{-}\). Then \(1 + \lambda_k^{-1} > \lambda^{\star}\), so the strict case applies to each \(\lambda_k\). The corresponding hardcore measures converge to \(\mu_{G, \lambda}\), and the state space \(\+I\left(G\right)\) is finite. Passing to the limit proves the boundary case.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on a finite or countable state space \(\Omega\), and let \(T > 0\). A localization process for \(\mu\) is an \(\left(\+F_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, T\right]}\)-adapted \(\+P\left(\Omega\right)\)-valued process \(\left(\nu_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, T\right]}\) such that \(\nu_0 = \mu\), \(\nu_T = \delta_X\) for some \(X \sim \mu\), and \(\left(\*E_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right)_{t \in \left[0, T\right]}\) is an \(\left(\+F_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, T\right]}\)-martingale for every bounded \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb R\). A localization scheme is a rule assigning a localization process to each target measure in a prescribed class.
    \label{def:localization-scheme}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
The transition semigroup \(\left(P_u^{\-n}\right)_{u \ge 0}\) of the noising process is given by
    \[
    P_u^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n'\right) := \*{Pr}\left[\*Y_u = \*n' \mid \*Y_0 = \*n\right] = \prod_{i = 1}^d \-{Bin}\left(n_i, e^{-u}; n_i'\right), \quad \forall \*n, \*n' \in \mathbb N^d, \, u \ge 0.
    \]
    \label{prop:noising-transition-semigroup}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since the coordinates evolve independently, it suffices to show that, for each \(i \in \left[d\right]\),
    \[
    \*{Pr}\left[Y_{v + u, i} = n_i' \mid Y_{v, i} = n_i\right] = \-{Bin}\left(n_i, e^{-u}; n_i'\right), \quad n_i, n_i' \in \mathbb N, \quad u, v \ge 0.
    \]
    Couple \(\left(Y_{u, i}\right)_{u \ge 0}\) to a system of independently dying particles. Conditional on \(Y_{v, i} = n_i\), let each of the \(n_i\) particles die independently at rate \(1\). Each particle survives from time \(v\) to time \(v + u\) with probability \(e^{-u}\), and the linear death dynamics of \(Y_{u, i}\) coincide with those of the number of surviving particles. Hence \(Y_{v + u, i}\) has distribution \(\-{Bin}\left(n_i, e^{-u}\right)\) conditional on \(Y_{v, i} = n_i\).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
For \(0 < s \le t \le 1\), the denoising process \(\left(\*X_t\right)_{t \in \left(0, 1\right]}\) satisfies
    \[
    \*{Pr}\left[\*X_s = \*n' \mid \*X_t = \*n\right] = \prod_{i = 1}^d \-{Bin}\left(n_i, \frac{s}{t}; n_i'\right), \quad \forall \*n, \*n' \in \mathbb N^d.
    \]
    \label{prop:noising-transition-semigroup-denoising}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
The denoising process \(\left(\*X_t\right)_{t \in \left(0, 1\right]}\) is a time-inhomogeneous Markov process with generator
    \begin{equation}
        \+L_t^{\-d} f\left(\*n\right) := \sum_{i = 1}^d q_{t, i}\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right), \quad t \in \left(0, 1\right),
        \label{eq:denoising-generator}
    \end{equation}
    where
    \[
    q_{t, i}\left(\*n\right) := \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu_t\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{t \mu_t\left(\*n\right)}, \qquad \mu_t := \-{Law}\left(\*X_t\right).
    \]
    \label{prop:denoising-generator}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Fix \(t \in \left(0, 1\right)\), \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu_t\right)\), and \(i \in \left[d\right]\). For \(h > 0\) such that \(t + h \le 1\), Bayes' rule and \Cref{prop:noising-transition-semigroup} give
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*{Pr}\left[\*X_{t + h} = \*n + \*e_i \mid \*X_t = \*n\right]
        &= \frac{\mu_{t + h}\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu_t\left(\*n\right)} \*{Pr}\left[\*X_t = \*n \mid \*X_{t + h} = \*n + \*e_i\right] \\
        &= \frac{\mu_{t + h}\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu_t\left(\*n\right)} \left(n_i + 1\right) \left(\frac{t}{t + h}\right)^{\sum_{j = 1}^d n_j} \frac{h}{t + h}.
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Therefore,
    \[
    \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{1}{h} \*{Pr}\left[\*X_{t + h} = \*n + \*e_i \mid \*X_t = \*n\right] = \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu_t\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{t \mu_t\left(\*n\right)} = q_{t, i}\left(\*n\right).
    \]
    The denoising process cannot jump downward, and the probability of two or more births during \(\left[t, t + h\right]\) is \(o\left(h\right)\). Hence its only off-diagonal jump rates are \(q_{t, i}\left(\*n\right)\), which yields \eqref{eq:denoising-generator}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
The birth rates \(\left(\*q_t\left(\*X_t\right)\right)_{t \in \left(0, 1\right]}\) form a martingale with respect to the natural filtration generated by the denoising process \(\left(\*X_t\right)_{t \in \left(0, 1\right]}\).
    \label{prop:denoising-birth-rates-martingale}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
For \(0 < s \le t \le 1\), define the noising kernel from time \(t\) back to time \(s\) by
    \[
    Q_{t \to s}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n'\right) := \*{Pr}\left[\*X_s = \*n' \mid \*X_t = \*n\right] = \prod_{i = 1}^d \-{Bin}\left(n_i, \frac{s}{t}; n_i'\right).
    \]
    For \(\*n' \le \*n\) and \(i \in \left[d\right]\), the binomial identity
    \[
    \frac{n_i + 1}{t} Q_{t \to s}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n'\right) = \frac{n_i' + 1}{s} Q_{t \to s}^{\-n}\left(\*n + \*e_i, \*n' + \*e_i\right)
    \]
    holds. Thus, for every \(\*n' \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu_s\right)\),
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \*E\left[q_{t, i}\left(\*X_t\right) \mid \*X_s = \*n'\right]
        &= \sum_{\*n \ge \*n'} \frac{\mu_t\left(\*n\right) Q_{t \to s}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n'\right)}{\mu_s\left(\*n'\right)} \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu_t\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{t \mu_t\left(\*n\right)} \\
        &= \frac{n_i' + 1}{s \mu_s\left(\*n'\right)} \sum_{\*n \ge \*n'} \mu_t\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) Q_{t \to s}^{\-n}\left(\*n + \*e_i, \*n' + \*e_i\right) \\
        &= \frac{\left(n_i' + 1\right) \mu_s\left(\*n' + \*e_i\right)}{s \mu_s\left(\*n'\right)} \\
        &= q_{s, i}\left(\*n'\right).
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    In the first equality, we used Bayes' rule; in the third, we used the transition formula from \(t\) back to \(s\). The Markov property therefore gives
    \[
    \*E\left[\*q_t\left(\*X_t\right) \mid \+F_s\right] = \*E\left[\*q_t\left(\*X_t\right) \mid \*X_s\right] = \*q_s\left(\*X_s\right),
    \]
    where \(\left(\+F_t\right)_{t \in \left(0, 1\right]}\) is the natural filtration of the denoising process.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
The birth rates of the denoising process admit the conditional-expectation representation
    \[
    \*q_t\left(\*X_t\right) = \frac{1}{1 - t} \*E\left[\*X_1 - \*X_t \mid \*X_t\right], \quad t \in \left(0, 1\right).
    \]
    \label{cor:denoising-birth-rates-conditional-expectation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The compensated process
    \[
    \*X_u - \int_t^u \*q_s\left(\*X_s\right) \,\-d s, \quad u \in \left[t, 1\right],
    \]
    is a martingale. Hence, for \(t \in \left(0, 1\right)\),
    \[
    \*E\left[\*X_1 - \*X_t \mid \+F_t\right] = \int_t^1 \*E\left[\*q_s\left(\*X_s\right) \mid \+F_t\right] \,\-d s = \int_t^1 \*q_t\left(\*X_t\right) \,\-d s = \left(1 - t\right) \*q_t\left(\*X_t\right),
    \]
    where the second equality follows from \Cref{prop:denoising-birth-rates-martingale}. Since the denoising process is Markov, conditioning on \(\+F_t\) can be replaced by conditioning on \(\*X_t\), which proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Poisson stochastic localization is the localization scheme that assigns \(\left(\nu_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, 1\right]}\) to each target measure \(\mu\).
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
Let \(\left(\*M_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, 1\right]}\) be the compensated birth process defined coordinatewise by
    \[
    \,\-d M_{t, i} := \,\-d X_{t, i} - q_{t, i}\left(\*X_{t-}\right) \,\-d t.
    \]
    Define \(\left(\*Z_t\right)_{t \in \left[0, 1\right]}\) by \(Z_{0, i} := 0\) and
    \[
    \,\-d Z_{t, i} :=
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle \frac{\,\-d M_{t, i}}{\!{mean}\left(\nu_{t-}\right)_i - X_{t-, i}}, & \!{mean}\left(\nu_{t-}\right)_i > X_{t-, i}, \\
        0, & \!{mean}\left(\nu_{t-}\right)_i = X_{t-, i}.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    Then \(\*Z_t\) is a martingale on every interval \(\left[0, T\right]\) with \(T < 1\), and Poisson stochastic localization satisfies the linear-tilt equation
    \[
    \,\-d \nu_t\left(\*n\right) = \nu_{t-}\left(\*n\right) \left\langle\*n - \!{mean}\left(\nu_{t-}\right),\,\,\-d \*Z_t\right\rangle, \quad \forall \*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right), \, t \in \left(0, 1\right).
    \]
    \label{thm:poisson-linear-tilt}
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
Let \(\Phi\) be a differentiable convex function on an interval \(I\), and let \(f \in \+C_{\-{c}}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) satisfy \(f\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right) \subseteq I\). Define
    \[
    \Psi\left(u, v\right) := \Phi\left(u + v\right) - \Phi\left(u\right) - v \Phi'\left(u\right).
    \]
    Then
    \[
    \,\-d \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}^{\Phi}\left[f\right]\right] = -\frac{1}{1 - t} \*E\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \left(\!{mean}\left(\nu_t\right)_i - X_{t, i}\right) \Psi\left(\*E_{\nu_t}\left[f\right], \frac{\*{Cov}_{\*n \sim \nu_t}\left[f\left(\*n\right), n_i\right]}{\!{mean}\left(\nu_t\right)_i - X_{t, i}}\right)\right] \,\-d t.
    \]
    In particular:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(\Phi\left(x\right) = x^2\), then
        \[
        \,\-d \*E\left[\*{Var}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] = -\frac{1}{1 - t} \*E\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\*{Cov}_{\*n \sim \nu_t}\left[f\left(\*n\right), n_i\right]^2}{\!{mean}\left(\nu_t\right)_i - X_{t, i}}\right] \,\-d t.
        \]
        \item If \(\Phi\left(x\right) = x \log x\) and \(f \ge 0\), then
        \[
        \,\-d \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] = -\frac{1}{1 - t} \*E\left[\*E_{\nu_t}\left[f\right] \sum_{i = 1}^d \Psi\left(\!{mean}\left(\nu_t\right)_i - X_{t, i}, \frac{\*{Cov}_{\*n \sim \nu_t}\left[f\left(\*n\right), n_i\right]}{\*E_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]}\right)\right] \,\-d t,
        \]
        with the convention \(0 \log 0 := 0\).
    \end{itemize}
    Every quotient with zero denominator is interpreted as zero; the corresponding covariance then also vanishes.
    \label{thm:phi-entropy-evolution}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let \(\gamma_t\) and \(\rho_t\) be defined as in \eqref{eq:approximate-conservation-constants}. Then \(Q_{1 \leftrightarrow t}\) satisfies the Poincar\'e\xspace inequality with constant \(\gamma_t\) and the modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\rho_t\):
    \[
    \gamma_t \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \+E_{Q_{1 \leftrightarrow t}}\left(f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right),
    \]
    \[
    \rho_t \, \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \+E_{Q_{1 \leftrightarrow t}}\left(\log f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right), \, f \ge 0,
    \]
    and the constant \(\gamma_t\) is the optimal Poincar\'e\xspace constant.
    \label{lem:associated-markov-chain-functional-inequalities}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
Suppose that the target distribution \(\mu\) is supported on a downward closed subset of \(\mathbb N^d\). For \(t \in \left(0, 1\right)\), set \(\+L^{Q_{1 \leftrightarrow t}} := Q_{1 \leftrightarrow t} - I\). For \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) and \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), define
    \[
    \+L f\left(\*n\right) := \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \+L^{Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon}} f\left(\*n\right).
    \]
    Then
    \[
    \+L f\left(\*n\right) = \sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) + \sum_{i = 1}^d n_i \nabla_i^- f\left(\*n\right),
    \]
    which coincides with \eqref{eq:birth-death-generator}.
    \label{thm:associated-limiting-process}
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Set \(b_i\left(\*n\right) := \left(n_i + 1\right)\mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)/\mu\left(\*n\right)\). We first compute the transition rates of \(Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon}\). For each fixed \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), \Cref{prop:noising-transition-semigroup-denoising} gives
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        Q_{1 \to 1 - \varepsilon}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n\right) &= 1 - \varepsilon \left\|\*n\right\|_1 + O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \\
        Q_{1 \to 1 - \varepsilon}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*n - \*e_i\right) &= \varepsilon n_i + O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \quad i \in \left[d\right], \, n_i > 0,
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    while the total probability of two or more deaths is \(O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)\).
    
    The reverse kernel is the posterior \(Q_{1 - \varepsilon \to 1}^{\-d}\left(\*x, \cdot\right) = \nu_{1 - \varepsilon, \*x}\). For fixed \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), \Cref{prop:noising-transition-semigroup-denoising} yields
    \[
    \mu_{1 - \varepsilon}\left(\*x\right) = \left(\mu Q_{1 \to 1 - \varepsilon}^{\-n}\right) \left(\*x\right) = \left(1 - \varepsilon\right)^{\left\|\*x\right\|_1} \left[\mu\left(\*x\right) + \varepsilon \sum_{i = 1}^d \left(x_i + 1\right)\mu\left(\*x + \*e_i\right) + O_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)\right].
    \]
    This expansion remains valid when \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) is infinite. Specifically, for \(\*n = \*x + \*k\), we have
    \[
    Q_{1 \to 1 - \varepsilon}^{\-n}\left(\*n, \*x\right) = \prod_{i = 1}^d \binom{x_i + k_i}{x_i} \left(1 - \varepsilon\right)^{x_i} \varepsilon^{k_i} = \left(1 - \varepsilon\right)^{\left\|\*x\right\|_1} \varepsilon^{\left\|\*k\right\|_1} \prod_{i = 1}^d \binom{x_i + k_i}{x_i}.
    \]
    Note that \(\prod_i \binom{x_i + k_i}{x_i}\) grows only polynomially in \(\*k\), whereas \(\varepsilon^{\left\|\*k\right\|_1}\) decays geometrically. Consequently, the sum over terms with \(\left\|\*k\right\|_1 \ge 2\) is \(O_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)\). Substituting this into the expression for \(\nu_{1 - \varepsilon, \*x}\) gives
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
            Q_{1 - \varepsilon \to 1}^{\-d}\left(\*x, \*x\right) &= 1 - \varepsilon \sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*x\right) + O_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \\
            Q_{1 - \varepsilon \to 1}^{\-d}\left(\*x, \*x + \*e_i\right) &= \varepsilon b_i\left(\*x\right) + O_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \quad i \in \left[d\right],
        \end{aligned}
        \label{eq:posterior-expansion}
    \end{equation}
    with total remaining posterior mass \(O_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)\).
    
    Composing the two kernels, we obtain
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon}\left(\*n, \*n - \*e_i\right) &= \varepsilon n_i + O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \quad i \in \left[d\right] \\
        Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon}\left(\*n, \*n + \*e_i\right) &= \varepsilon b_i\left(\*n\right) + O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right), \quad i \in \left[d\right] \\
        Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon}\left(\*n, \*n\right) &= 1 - \varepsilon \sum_{i = 1}^d \left(n_i + b_i\left(\*n\right)\right) + O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right),
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    with total remaining mass \(O_{\*n}\left(\varepsilon^2\right)\). Hence, for every \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) and \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\),
    \[
    \+L f\left(\*n\right) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\left(Q_{1 \leftrightarrow 1 - \varepsilon} - I\right)f\left(\*n\right)}{\varepsilon} = \sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right)\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right) + \sum_{i = 1}^d n_i \nabla_i^- f\left(\*n\right).
    \]
    This proves the asserted generator limit.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
Let \(\gamma_t\) and \(\rho_t\) be defined as in \eqref{eq:approximate-conservation-constants}, and suppose that \(\mu\) has downward closed support and finite first moments. Set
    \[
    \gamma := \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\gamma_{1 - \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \rho := \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\rho_{1 - \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon}.
    \]
    Then \(\mu\) satisfies the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality:
    \[
    \gamma \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] = \+E\left(f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+D\left(\+E\right),
    \]
    and the weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality:
    \[
    \rho \, \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \Psi\left(f\left(\*n\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right] \le \+E\left(\log f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+A.
    \]
    Here, \(\+E\left(\cdot, \cdot\right)\) is the Dirichlet form of \(\+L\) defined as in \eqref{eq:birth-death-dirichlet-form}, and \(\Psi\left(u, v\right) := \left(u + v\right) \log\left(u + v\right) - u \log u - v \left(\log u + 1\right)\) with the convention \(\Psi\left(0, 0\right) = 0\). The corresponding domains are
    \[
    \+D\left(\+E\right) := \left\{f \in L^2\left(\mu\right) \,:\, \+E\left(f, f\right) < \infty\right\}, \qquad \+A := \left\{f \in L^2\left(\mu\right) \,:\, f > 0, \, f \in \+D\left(\+E\right), \, \log f \in \+D\left(\+E\right)\right\}.
    \]
    \label{thm:limiting-process-functional-inequalities}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The modified log-Sobolev inequality obtained above is stronger than the standard inequality involving \(\+E\left(\log f, f\right)\). Such an inequality was first introduced by Wu \cite{Wu00}. A more detailed discussion of this class of functional inequalities is deferred to \Cref{subsec:ulc-mlsi}.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let \(\Phi\) be differentiable and convex, and write
    \[
    \Psi_{\Phi}\left(u, v\right) := \Phi\left(u + v\right) - \Phi\left(u\right) - v \Phi'\left(u\right).
    \]
    It suffices initially to take \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\). For \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), the posterior expansion \eqref{eq:posterior-expansion} and the differentiability of \(\Phi\) give
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\nu_{1 - \varepsilon, \*x}}^{\Phi}\left[f\right] = \varepsilon \sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*x\right) \Psi_{\Phi}\left(f\left(\*x\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*x\right)\right) + o_{\*x}\left(\varepsilon\right).
    \]
    Write \(S_f := \left\{\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right) \,:\, \exists \*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(f\right), \, \*n \ge \*x\right\}\). Note that \(S_f\) is finite, and \(\*{Ent}_{\nu_{1 - \varepsilon, \*x}}^{\Phi}\left[f\right] = 0\) for \(\*x \notin S_f\). Hence, using \(\mu_{1 - \varepsilon}\left(\*x\right) \to \mu\left(\*x\right)\) and summing over \(\*x \in S_f\) yields
    \[
    \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_{1 - \varepsilon}}^{\Phi}\left[f\right]\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \Psi_{\Phi}\left(f\left(\*n\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right].
    \]
    
    Taking \(\Phi\left(x\right) = x^2\) and using the definition of \(\gamma_{1 - \varepsilon}\), we have
    \[
    \frac{\gamma_{1 - \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon} \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \*E\left[\*{Var}_{\nu_{1 - \varepsilon}}\left[f\right]\right].
    \]
    Passing to the lower limit gives
    \[
    \gamma \, \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \left(\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] = \+E\left(f, f\right).
    \]
    Likewise, for \(\Phi\left(x\right) = x \log x\) and nonnegative \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\),
    \[
    \rho \, \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \Psi\left(f\left(\*n\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right].
    \]
    By the elementary inequality \(\Psi\left(u, v\right) \le v \left(\log\left(u + v\right) - \log u\right)\),
    \[
    \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \Psi\left(f\left(\*n\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ \log f\left(\*n\right) \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right] = \+E\left(\log f, f\right).
    \]
    
    Finally, the finite-first-moment assumption implies
    \[
    \sum_{\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)} \mu\left(\*n\right) \sum_{i = 1}^d b_i\left(\*n\right) = \*E_{\mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d n_i\right] < \infty.
    \]
    Thus, truncation in value followed by restriction to the coordinate boxes \(S_N\) from the proof of \Cref{thm:ulc-poincare-inequality} shows that \(\+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) is a core for \(\+D\left(\+E\right)\), while the non-negative \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\) form a core for \(\+A\). The boundary contributions vanish by the preceding finite-conductance identity. Passing to the limit extends the two inequalities to the stated domains.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\). We say that \(\mu\) is \(\eta\)-spectrally independent with respect to Poisson stochastic localization if
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \preceq \eta \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\right).
    \]
    Unless otherwise specified, we refer to this property simply as spectral independence.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
This definition differs slightly from the standard notion of spectral independence. In particular, when \(\mu\) is supported on a subset of \(\left\{0,1\right\}^d\), the standard definition requires
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \preceq \left(1 + \eta\right) \operatorname{diag}\left(\*{Var}_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[n_i\right]\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}.
    \]
    In the \(\left\{0, 1\right\}^d\) setting, our spectral independence is slightly weaker than the standard one. This difference reflects the distinct localization schemes underlying the two notions: ours arises naturally from Poisson stochastic localization, whereas the standard notion is induced by coordinate-by-coordinate localization.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\) with downward closed support. Write \(\ell_{\*v}\left(\*x\right) := \*v^{\top} \*x\). Then \(\mu\) is \(\eta\)-spectrally independent if and only if \(\mu\) satisfies the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality for the class of linear functions with constant \(1 / \eta\):
    \[
    \frac{1}{\eta} \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[\ell_{\*v}\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ \ell_{\*v}\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right], \quad \forall \*v \in \mathbb R^d \setminus\left\{\*0\right\}.
    \]
    \label{prop:spectral-independence-weighted-poincare}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The Dirichlet form satisfies
    \[
    \+E\left(f, f\right) = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \left(\nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right] = \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d n_i \left(\nabla_i^- f\left(\*n\right)\right)^2\right].
    \]
    Thus, for any \(\*v \in \mathbb R^d \setminus \left\{\*0\right\}\), the weighted Poincar\'e\xspace inequality for \(\ell_{\*v}\) is equivalent to
    \[
    \*v^{\top} \!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \*v = \*{Var}_{\mu}\left[\ell_{\*v}\right] \le \eta \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d n_i v_i^2\right] = \eta \sum_{i = 1}^d \!{mean}\left(\mu\right)_i v_i^2 = \eta \*v^{\top} \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\right) \*v.
    \]
    Since this holds for every \(\*v \in \mathbb R^d \setminus \left\{\*0\right\}\) if and only if \(\!{cov}\left(\mu\right) \preceq \eta \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\right)\), the result follows.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
Every \(\delta\)-ULC probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb N^d\) is \(1/\delta\)-spectrally independent.
    \label{cor:ulc-cov-bound}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\). For \(\*x \in \Omega\), the weighted pinning of \(\mu\) at \(\*x\) is the probability measure defined by
    \[
    \mu^{\*x}\left(\*k\right) \propto \mu\left(\*x + \*k\right) \prod_{i = 1}^d \binom{x_i + k_i}{x_i}, \quad \*k \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \*x + \*k \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
    \label{def:weighted-pinning}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
The definition becomes more transparent in factorial-weighted form:
    \[
    \*k! \mu^{\*x}\left(\*k\right) \propto \left(\*x + \*k\right)! \mu\left(\*x + \*k\right), \quad \*k \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \*x + \*k \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right).
    \]
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
Fix \(t \in \left[0, 1\right)\). Suppose that \(\left(1 - t\right) * \mu^{\*x}\) is \(\eta_t\)-spectrally independent for every \(\*x \in \Omega\). Then, for every \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\),
    \[
    \partial_t \*E\left[\*{Var}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] \ge -\frac{\eta_t}{1 - t} \*E\left[\*{Var}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right].
    \]
    Moreover, suppose that \(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\) is \(\eta\)-spectrally independent for every \(\*x \in \Omega\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Then, for every nonnegative \(f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right)\),
    \[
    \partial_t \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] \ge -\frac{\eta}{1 - t} \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right], \quad \forall t \in \left[0, 1\right).
    \]
    \label{prop:sufficient-condition-approximate-conservation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
ULC is preserved under weighted pinning and exponential tilting. More precisely, if \(\mu\) is ULC, then \(\mu^{\*x}\) is ULC for every \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu\) is ULC for every \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\).
    \label{lem:ulc-closure-pinning-exponential-tilt}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Write \(a\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\). For \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), the factorial-weighted mass function of \(\mu^{\*x}\) satisfies
    \[
    a_{\*x}\left(\*k\right) := \*k! \mu^{\*x}\left(\*k\right) = c_{\*x} a\left(\*x + \*k\right)
    \]
    for some \(c_{\*x} > 0\). The support of \(\mu^{\*x}\) is downward closed, and its active coordinates at \(\*k\) are exactly those of \(\mu\) at \(\*x + \*k\). Moreover, for every pair of active coordinates \(i, j\),
    \[
    \frac{a_{\*x}\left(\*k\right) a_{\*x}\left(\*k + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a_{\*x}\left(\*k + \*e_i\right) a_{\*x}\left(\*k + \*e_j\right)} = \frac{a\left(\*x + \*k\right) a\left(\*x + \*k + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*x + \*k + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*x + \*k + \*e_j\right)}.
    \]
    Thus the local curvature matrix of \(\mu^{\*x}\) at \(\*k\) equals that of \(\mu\) at \(\*x + \*k\), so \(\mu^{\*x}\) is ULC.

    Now fix \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\) and set \(\widetilde{\mu} := \boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu\). For its normalizing constant \(Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\),
    \[
    \widetilde{a}\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \widetilde{\mu}\left(\*n\right) = Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*n} a\left(\*n\right), \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*n} := \prod_{i = 1}^d \theta_i^{n_i}.
    \]
    The tilt has the same support as \(\mu\), and the geometric factor cancels from each ratio in the ULC matrix:
    \[
    \frac{\widetilde{a}\left(\*n\right) \widetilde{a}\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{\widetilde{a}\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) \widetilde{a}\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)} = \frac{a\left(\*n\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j\right)}{a\left(\*n + \*e_i\right) a\left(\*n + \*e_j\right)}.
    \]
    Hence \(\widetilde{\mu}\) has the same ULC matrix as \(\mu\) at every state and is therefore ULC.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
Every ULC probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb N^d\) with finite first moments satisfies the weighted Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(1\):
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{\*n \sim \mu}\left[\sum_{i = 1}^d \frac{\left(n_i + 1\right) \mu\left(\*n + \*e_i\right)}{\mu\left(\*n\right)} \Psi\left(f\left(\*n\right), \nabla_i^+ f\left(\*n\right)\right)\right] \le \+E\left(\log f, f\right), \quad \forall f \in \+A.
    \]
    Here, \(\Psi\left(u, v\right) := \left(u + v\right) \log\left(u + v\right) - u \log u - v \left(\log u + 1\right)\), with \(\Psi\left(0, 0\right) := 0\), and \(\+E\) and \(\+A\) are defined in \Cref{thm:limiting-process-functional-inequalities}.
    \label{thm:ulc-modified-log-sobolev-inequality}
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Fix \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). By \Cref{lem:ulc-closure-pinning-exponential-tilt}, \(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\) is ULC, and hence \Cref{cor:ulc-cov-bound} gives
    \[
    \!{cov}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\right) \preceq \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\right)\right).
    \]
    Applying \Cref{prop:sufficient-condition-approximate-conservation} with \(\eta = 1\) yields
    \[
    \partial_t \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] \ge -\frac{1}{1 - t} \*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right], \quad \forall t \in \left[0, 1\right).
    \]
    Integrating this differential inequality gives \(\*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right] \ge \left(1 - t\right) \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right]\), and therefore
    \[
    \rho_t = \inf_{\substack{f \in \+C_{\-c}\left(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\right), \, f \ge 0 \\ \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] > 0}} \frac{\*E\left[\*{Ent}_{\nu_t}\left[f\right]\right]}{\*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right]} \ge \exp\left(-\int_0^t \frac{1}{1 - s} \,\-d s\right) = 1 - t.
    \]
    Consequently, \Cref{thm:limiting-process-functional-inequalities} gives the claimed inequality because
    \[
    \rho = \liminf_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\rho_{1 - \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon} \ge 1.
    \]
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
Wu's modified log-Sobolev inequality \cite{Wu00} is the Poisson-space counterpart of \Cref{thm:ulc-modified-log-sobolev-inequality}. Let \(\mathbb P\) be the law of a Poisson point process on a measurable space \(X\) with intensity measure \(\nu\), and define the add-one operator by \(D_z F\left(\omega\right) := F\left(\omega + \delta_z\right) - F\left(\omega\right)\). Then, for every suitable nonnegative functional \(F\),
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\mathbb P}\left[F\right] \le \*E_{\mathbb P}\left[\int_X \Psi\left(F, D_z F\right) \nu\left(\-d z\right)\right].
    \]
    At least informally, Wu's inequality can be recovered from \Cref{thm:ulc-modified-log-sobolev-inequality} by identifying a simple point configuration on \(X\) with its indicator in the infinite-dimensional hypercube \(\left\{0,1\right\}^X\). Under this identification, the add-one operator \(D_z\) is the continuum analogue of the discrete coordinatewise increment \(\nabla_z^+\), and the Poisson law is ULC in the corresponding infinite-dimensional sense. Applying \Cref{thm:ulc-modified-log-sobolev-inequality} therefore yields Wu's modified log-Sobolev inequality on Poisson space.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
In one dimension, \Cref{thm:ulc-modified-log-sobolev-inequality} specializes to
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \*E_{n \sim \mu}\left[\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \mu\left(n + 1\right)}{\mu\left(n\right)} \Psi\left(f\left(n\right), \nabla^+ f\left(n\right)\right)\right], \quad \forall f \in \+A.
    \]
    Since \(a\left(n\right) := n! \mu\left(n\right)\) is log-concave, the birth rates
    \[
    \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \mu\left(n + 1\right)}{\mu\left(n\right)} = \frac{a\left(n + 1\right)}{a\left(n\right)}, \quad n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right),
    \]
    are non-increasing in \(n\). In particular, they are bounded above by \(\mu\left(1\right) / \mu\left(0\right)\). The weighted inequality therefore implies the standard Wu-type modified log-Sobolev inequality
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] \le \frac{\mu\left(1\right)}{\mu\left(0\right)} \*E_{\mu}\left[\Psi\left(f, \nabla^+ f\right)\right], \quad \forall f \in \+A.
    \]
    This recovers \cite[Theorem~1.3]{Joh17}. L\'opez-Rivera and Shenfeld subsequently improved the constant \(\mu\left(1\right) / \mu\left(0\right)\) to \(\left|\log \mu\left(0\right)\right|\) and conjectured that it could be further improved to \(\!{mean}\left(\mu\right)\) \cite{LRS25}. We note that their conjecture is false and that \(\left|\log \mu\left(0\right)\right|\) is the sharp constant. Indeed, applying the inequality to \(f := \delta_0\) yields 
    \[
    \*{Ent}_{\mu}\left[f\right] = \mu\left(0\right)\left|\log \mu\left(0\right)\right|, \qquad \*E_{\mu}\left[\Psi\left(f, \nabla^+ f\right)\right] = \mu\left(0\right).
    \] 
    Thus, any admissible constant must be at least \(\left|\log \mu\left(0\right)\right|\).
    \label{ex:one-dim-ulc-mlsi}
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\). Its probability-generating function is the formal power series
    \[
    g_{\mu}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) := \sum_{\*n \in \mathbb N^d} \mu\left(\*n\right) \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*n}.
    \]
    When \(\mu\) has finite support, \(g_{\mu}\) is its generating polynomial. Following \cite{Gur09a}, we say that \(g_{\mu}\) is strongly log-concave if, for every \(\*x \in \mathbb N^d\),
    \[
    \partial^{\*x} g_{\mu} := \partial_1^{x_1} \cdots \partial_d^{x_d} g_{\mu}
    \]
    is either identically zero or finite, positive, and log-concave on \(\mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Following \cite{AOGV21}, we say that \(g_{\mu}\) is completely log-concave if, for every \(k \in \mathbb N\) and \(\*v_1, \dots, \*v_k \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^d\),
    \[
    \partial_{\*v_1} \dots \partial_{\*v_k} g_{\mu}
    \]
    is either identically zero or finite, positive, and log-concave on \(\mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Here \(\partial_{\*v} := \sum_{i = 1}^d v_i \partial_i\) denotes the directional derivative in the direction of \(\*v\).
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\) with downward closed support. Then the following statements are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The measure \(\mu\) is ultra-log-concave.
        \item For every \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) and \(t \in \left[0, 1\right)\), the tilted pinning \(\left(1 - t\right) * \mu^{\*x}\) is \(1\)-spectrally independent.
        \item For every \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\), the tilted pinning \(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\) is \(1\)-spectrally independent.
        \item The probability-generating function \(g_{\mu}\) is strongly log-concave.
        \item The probability-generating function \(g_{\mu}\) is completely log-concave.
    \end{enumerate}
    \label{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization}
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
We prove here only the equivalence of Items~1--4. Establishing the equivalence with Item~5 requires an appropriate homogenization of \(g_{\mu}\), together with the theory of Lorentzian polynomials developed in \cite{BH20}. Since the implication \(5 \Rightarrow 4\) is immediate, it remains only to establish \(1 \Rightarrow 5\); we defer its proof to \Cref{subsec:ulc-completely-log-concavity}.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The implication \(3 \Rightarrow 2\) is immediate. Write \(a\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\). For \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), define
    \[
    h_{\*x}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) := \partial^{\*x} g_{\mu}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) = \sum_{\*k \in \mathbb N^d} \frac{a\left(\*x + \*k\right)}{\*k!} \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*k}.
    \]
    Write \(\mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}} := \boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu^{\*x}\). Since
    \[
    \mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\*k\right) \propto \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*k} \mu\left(\*x + \*k\right) \prod_{i = 1}^d \binom{x_i + k_i}{x_i} \propto \frac{a\left(\*x + \*k\right) \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*k}}{\*k!},
    \]
    we have
    \[
    \mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\*k\right) = \frac{a\left(\*x + \*k\right) \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*k}}{\*k! \, h_{\*x}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)}.
    \]
    Differentiating the log-partition function gives
    \begin{equation}
        \nabla^2 \log h_{\*x}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) = \operatorname{diag}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)^{-1} \left(\!{cov}\left(\mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\right) - \operatorname{diag}\left(\!{mean}\left(\mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)\right)\right) \operatorname{diag}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)^{-1}.
        \label{eq:tilted-pinning-log-hessian}
    \end{equation}

    \paragraph{\(1 \Rightarrow 3\).} Suppose that \(\mu\) is ULC. By \Cref{lem:ulc-closure-pinning-exponential-tilt}, \(\mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\) is ULC for every \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Hence, by \Cref{cor:ulc-cov-bound}, \(\mu^{\*x, \boldsymbol{\theta}}\) is \(1\)-spectrally independent.
