For every \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\), the measure \(\mu\) is ULC if and only if its relative density with respect to \(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} := \bigotimes_{i = 1}^d \-{Pois}\left(\lambda_i\right)\) is log-concave in the sense of \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity}.
    \label{prop:ulc-poisson-relative-log-concavity}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Write \(a\left(\*n\right) := \*n! \mu\left(\*n\right)\). Since
    \[
    \frac{\,\-d \mu}{\,\-d \pi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\left(\*n\right) = e^{\left\|\boldsymbol{\lambda}\right\|_1} \frac{a\left(\*n\right)}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\*n}},
    \]
    the constant and geometric factors cancel from every ratio in \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity}. The resulting matrix is exactly the ULC matrix of \(\mu\).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
The class of ULC measures is closed under the following operations:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Exponential tilt:} If \(\mu\) is ULC, then for every \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\), the tilted measure \(\boldsymbol{\theta} * \mu\) is ULC.
        \item \textbf{Weighted pinning:} If \(\mu\) is ULC, then for every \(\*x \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\), the measure \(\mu^{\*x}\), as defined in \Cref{def:weighted-pinning}, is ULC.
        \item \textbf{Product:} If \(\mu^{\left(i\right)}\) is ULC for \(i = 1, 2, \dots, k\), then the product measure \(\bigotimes_{i = 1}^k \mu^{\left(i\right)}\) is ULC.
        \item \textbf{Box truncation:} If \(\mu\) is ULC on \(\mathbb N^d\), then for every \(\*N \in \mathbb N^d\), the measure \(\mu\) restricted to the box \(\left\{\*n \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \*n \le \*N\right\}\) is ULC.
        \item \textbf{Coordinate conditioning:} If \(\mu\) is ULC on \(\mathbb N^d\) and \(\*{Pr}_{\*X \sim \mu}\left[\*X_S = \*x\right] > 0\) for some \(S \subseteq \left[d\right]\) and \(\*x \in \mathbb N^S\), then \(\mu_{\left[d\right] \setminus S}^{S \gets \*x}\) is ULC.
    \end{itemize}
    \label{prop:ulc-basic-closure-properties}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
Weighted pinning, product, box truncation, and coordinate conditioning preserve not only ULC, but also \(\delta\)-ULC for the same \(\delta\).
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
If \(\mu\) is ULC on \(\mathbb N^d\), then for every \(S \subseteq \left[d\right]\), the marginal measure \(\mu_S\) is ULC.
    \label{prop:ulc-marginalization-closure}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
The support of \(\mu_S\) is downward closed, and
    \[
    g_{\mu_S}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_S\right) = g_{\mu}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}_S, \*1_{\left[d\right] \setminus S}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\theta}_S \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^S.
    \]
    Every partial derivative of \(g_{\mu_S}\) is therefore the restriction of the corresponding partial derivative of \(g_{\mu}\) to this affine subspace. Since restrictions of log-concave functions to affine subspaces are log-concave, \(g_{\mu_S}\) is strongly log-concave. The result follows from \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization}.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\). For \(\*p \in \left(0, 1\right]^d\), define the coordinatewise binomial thinning operator \(\+T_{\*p}\) by
    \begin{equation}
        \+T_{\*p} \mu := \-{Law}\left(\*X'\right), \qquad \*{Pr}\left[\*X' = \*n' \mid \*X = \*n\right] = \prod_{i = 1}^d \-{Bin}\left(n_i, p_i; n_i'\right), \qquad \*X \sim \mu.
        \label{eq:binomial-thinning-operator}
    \end{equation}
    In particular, for \(p \in \left(0, 1\right]\), we abbreviate \(\+T_{p \*1}\) as \(\+T_p\).
    \label{def:binomial-thinning-operator}
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
If \(\mu\) is ULC on \(\mathbb N^d\), then for every \(\*p \in \left(0, 1\right]^d\), the thinned measure \(\+T_{\*p} \mu\) is ULC.
    \label{prop:ulc-thinning-closure}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
The probability-generating function of \(\+T_{\*p} \mu\) is
    \[
    g_{\+T_{\*p} \mu}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) = g_{\mu}\left(\left(1 - p_i + p_i \theta_i\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}\right).
    \]
    Hence, for every \(\*x \in \mathbb N^d\),
    \[
    \partial^{\*x} g_{\+T_{\*p} \mu}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) = \*p^{\*x} \left(\partial^{\*x} g_{\mu}\right)\left(\left(1 - p_i + p_i \theta_i\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}\right).
    \]
    By \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization}, each nonzero \(\partial^{\*x} g_{\mu}\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Its composition with the displayed affine map is log-concave, so \(g_{\+T_{\*p} \mu}\) is strongly log-concave. The support of \(\+T_{\*p} \mu\) is downward closed, and applying \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization} completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
Let \(\left(P_t\right)_{t \ge 0}\) denote the semigroup of the pure birth process on \(\mathbb N^d\) with birth rates \(\*b = \left(b_1, \dots, b_d\right)\). If \(f: \mathbb N^d \to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) is log-concave, then \(P_t f\) is log-concave whenever it is finite. Here log-concavity is understood in the sense of \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity}.
    \label{cor:poisson-semigroup-preserves-log-concavity}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
The equivalence between \Cref{prop:ulc-thinning-closure} and \Cref{cor:poisson-semigroup-preserves-log-concavity} can also be established more intrinsically, using the fact that binomial thinning is the time reversal of the Poisson semigroup.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
The result is immediate if \(f\) is identically zero, so assume otherwise. For \(N \in \mathbb N\), let
    \[
    f_N\left(\*n\right) := f\left(\*n\right) \*1_{\left\{\*n \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \left\|\*n\right\|_{\infty} \le N\right\}}.
    \]
    Directly from \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity}, each \(f_N\) is log-concave. Fix an arbitrary \(\*q \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\), set \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} := \*q + t \*b\), and let \(\*p := \left(q_i / \lambda_i\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}\). Define
    \[
    \pi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}} := \bigotimes_{i = 1}^d \-{Pois}\left(\lambda_i\right), \qquad Z_N := \*E_{\pi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\left[f_N\right], \qquad \mu_N\left(\*n\right) := \frac{f_N\left(\*n\right) \pi_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\left(\*n\right)}{Z_N}.
    \]
    By \Cref{prop:ulc-poisson-relative-log-concavity}, \(\mu_N\) is ULC. Since \(\*p \in \left(0, 1\right]^d\), \Cref{prop:ulc-thinning-closure} shows that \(\+T_{\*p} \mu_N\) is ULC. A direct calculation using \(\lambda_i p_i = q_i\) and \(\lambda_i \left(1 - p_i\right) = b_i t\) gives
    \[
    \left(\+T_{\*p} \mu_N\right)\left(\*n\right) = \frac{\pi_{\*q}\left(\*n\right)}{Z_N} P_t f_N\left(\*n\right), \qquad \pi_{\*q} := \bigotimes_{i = 1}^d \-{Pois}\left(q_i\right).
    \]
    Thus \Cref{prop:ulc-poisson-relative-log-concavity} implies that \(P_t f_N\) is log-concave. As \(N \to \infty\), monotone convergence gives \(P_t f_N \to P_t f\) pointwise. The cone of positive semidefinite matrices is closed, so the inequalities in \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity} pass to the limit whenever \(P_t f\) is finite. Moreover, \(\operatorname{supp}\left(P_t f\right) = \operatorname{supp}\left(f\right)\), which is downward closed. Hence \(P_t f\) is log-concave.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- theorem-31: body_md -->
The class of ULC measures is closed under convolution. That is, if \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are ULC measures on \(\mathbb N^d\), then so is their convolution \(\mu * \nu\).
    \label{thm:ulc-convolution-closure}
<!-- end theorem-31 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
First suppose that \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) have finite support. Let \(\+H_N\) denote the homogenization operator introduced in \Cref{def:homogenized-generating-polynomial}. For every sufficiently large \(N\), define
    \[
    F_{\mu, N}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) := N! \, \+H_N g_{\mu}\left(1, \boldsymbol{\theta} / N\right) = \sum_{\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)} \mu\left(\*n\right) \frac{N!}{\left(N - \left\|\*n\right\|_1\right)! N^{\left\|\*n\right\|_1}} \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\*n},
    \]
    and define \(F_{\nu, N}\) analogously. By \Cref{lem:ulc-homogenization-lorentzian}, \(\+H_N g_{\mu}\) and \(\+H_N g_{\nu}\) are Lorentzian. Their product is Lorentzian by \cite[Corollary~2.32]{BH20}. By the equivalence between Lorentzian and homogeneous strongly log-concave polynomials \cite[Theorem~2.30]{BH20}, the product \(\+H_N g_{\mu} \+H_N g_{\nu}\) is strongly log-concave. Since strong log-concavity is preserved under restriction to \(\theta_0 = 1\), positive diagonal rescaling of the remaining variables, and multiplication by a positive constant, it follows that \(F_{\mu, N} F_{\nu, N}\) is strongly log-concave.

    As \(N \to \infty\), these polynomials and all their partial derivatives converge pointwise to those of \(g_{\mu} g_{\nu}\). Log-concavity of every derivative passes to the limit, so \(g_{\mu} g_{\nu}\) is strongly log-concave. Since \(g_{\mu * \nu} = g_{\mu} g_{\nu}\) and \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu * \nu\right)\) is downward closed, \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization} proves the claim for finite support.

    For general \(\mu\) and \(\nu\), let \(\mu_N\) and \(\nu_N\) be their normalized restrictions to \(\left\{\*n \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \left\|\*n\right\|_{\infty} \le N\right\}\). These measures are ULC by \Cref{prop:ulc-basic-closure-properties}, so \(\rho_N := \mu_N * \nu_N\) is ULC by the finite-support case. Let \(\Omega_N^{\mu}\) and \(\Omega_N^{\nu}\) denote the two restricted supports, and write \(\rho := \mu * \nu\). For each fixed \(\*n\), every \(\*m\) entering its ULC matrix satisfies, for sufficiently large \(N\),
    \[
    \rho_N\left(\*m\right) = \frac{\rho\left(\*m\right)}{\mu\left(\Omega_N^{\mu}\right) \nu\left(\Omega_N^{\nu}\right)}, \quad \forall \*m \in \left\{\*n\right\} \cup \left\{\*n + \*e_i \,:\, i \in \left[d\right]\right\} \cup \left\{\*n + \*e_i + \*e_j \,:\, i, j \in \left[d\right]\right\}.
    \]
    The common factor cancels from the local ratios, so the ULC matrices of \(\rho_N\) and \(\rho\) at \(\*n\) agree for all sufficiently large \(N\). Hence \(\rho\) is ULC.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
For \(f, g: \mathbb N^d \to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}\), their binomial convolution \(h\) is defined by
    \[
    h\left(\*n\right) := \sum_{\*0 \le \*k \le \*n} f\left(\*k\right) g\left(\*n - \*k\right) \prod_{i = 1}^d \binom{n_i}{k_i}, \quad \*n \in \mathbb N^d.
    \]
    \label{def:binomial-convolution}
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
Log-concavity is preserved under binomial convolution. That is, if \(f\) and \(g\) are log-concave in the sense of \eqref{eq:discrete-function-log-concavity}, then so is their binomial convolution \(h\).
    \label{cor:binomial-convolution-preserves-log-concavity}
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The claim is immediate if \(f\) or \(g\) is identically zero, so assume otherwise. Let \(f_N\) and \(g_N\) be their restrictions to \(\left\{\*n \in \mathbb N^d \,:\, \left\|\*n\right\|_{\infty} \le N\right\}\), and let \(h_N\) be their binomial convolution. Define
    \[
    A_N := \sum_{\*n \in \mathbb N^d} \frac{f_N\left(\*n\right)}{\*n!}, \qquad B_N := \sum_{\*n \in \mathbb N^d} \frac{g_N\left(\*n\right)}{\*n!}, \qquad \mu_N\left(\*n\right) := \frac{f_N\left(\*n\right)}{A_N \*n!}, \qquad \nu_N\left(\*n\right) := \frac{g_N\left(\*n\right)}{B_N \*n!}.
    \]
    The truncations \(f_N\) and \(g_N\) are log-concave, so \(\mu_N\) and \(\nu_N\) are ULC. By \Cref{thm:ulc-convolution-closure}, \(\rho_N := \mu_N * \nu_N\) is ULC, and
    \[
    \*n! \rho_N\left(\*n\right) = \frac{h_N\left(\*n\right)}{A_N B_N}.
    \]
    Thus \(h_N\) is log-concave. For every fixed \(\*n\), one has \(h_N\left(\*m\right) = h\left(\*m\right)\) for all sufficiently large \(N\) and every \(\*m\) entering the local matrix at \(\*n\). Hence the local matrices of \(h_N\) and \(h\) eventually agree. Since \(\operatorname{supp}\left(h\right) = \operatorname{supp}\left(f\right) + \operatorname{supp}\left(g\right)\) is downward closed, \(h\) is log-concave.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\), and let \(\*P \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{d \times m}\) satisfy \(\sum_{j = 1}^m P_{ij} \le 1\) for all \(i \in \left[d\right]\). The particlewise stochastic projection channel associated with \(\*P\) is defined as follows. Let \(\*X \sim \mu\) be the input. Conditional on \(\*X = \*n\), regard \(\*n\) as a configuration of \(d\) types of particles, with \(n_i\) particles of type \(i\). There are \(m\) possible output types. Independently, each particle of input type \(i\) is assigned output type \(j\) with probability \(P_{ij}\), and is discarded with probability \(1 - \sum_{j = 1}^m P_{ij}\). The output \(\*X' \in \mathbb N^m\) is the vector of resulting particle counts of the \(m\) output types.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
Particlewise stochastic projection preserves downward closed support. More precisely, let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb N^d\) with downward closed support, and let \(\nu\) be the output law of the particlewise stochastic projection channel associated with any feasible \(\*P\). Then \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right)\) is downward closed.
    \label{lem:stochastic-projection-downward-closed-support}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Let \(\*n' \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right)\). By definition, there exists \(\*n \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) together with a particlewise projection plan of positive probability that maps \(\*n\) to \(\*n'\). Fix any \(\*m' \le \*n'\). Starting from the same projection plan, remove precisely those input particles whose projected output particles are present in \(\*n'\) but not in \(\*m'\). Let \(\*m \le \*n\) be the resulting input configuration. Since \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\) is downward closed, \(\*m \in \operatorname{supp}\left(\mu\right)\). Applying the same projection choices to \(\*m\) produces exactly \(\*m'\), and this event still has positive probability. Therefore, \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right)\) is downward closed.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- theorem-32: body_md -->
Let \(\mu\) be a ULC measure on \(\mathbb N^d\), and let \(\*P \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{d \times m}\) satisfy \(\sum_{j = 1}^m P_{ij} \le 1\) for all \(i \in \left[d\right]\). Suppose that \(\*X \sim \mu\), and let \(\*X'\) be the output of the particlewise stochastic projection channel associated with \(\*P\). Then \(\nu := \-{Law}\left(\*X'\right)\) is ULC on \(\mathbb N^m\).
    \label{thm:ulc-stochastic-projection-closure}
<!-- end theorem-32 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
We prove a slightly more general statement. Let \(\*A \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{d \times m}\) and \(\*b \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^d\) satisfy \(\sum_{j = 1}^m A_{ij} + b_i > 0\) for all \(i \in \left[d\right]\). We claim that
    \[
    h\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) := \frac{g_{\mu}\left(\*A \boldsymbol{\theta} + \*b\right)}{g_{\mu}\left(\*A \*1 + \*b\right)}, \quad \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R^m
    \]
    is the probability-generating function of a ULC measure on \(\mathbb N^m\). The particlewise stochastic projection channel is the special case
    \[
    \*A = \*P, \qquad \*b = \left(1 - \sum_{j = 1}^m P_{ij}\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}.
    \]

    Since \(g_{\mu}\) has nonnegative coefficients, so does \(h\), and \(h\left(\*1\right) = 1\). Hence \(h\) is the probability-generating function of some probability measure \(\nu\) on \(\mathbb N^m\). Set
    \[
    \*r := \left(r_i\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}, \qquad r_i := \sum_{j = 1}^m A_{ij} + b_i, \quad i \in \left[d\right],
    \]
    and define
    \[
    \widetilde{\*P}_{ij} := \frac{A_{ij}}{r_i}, \quad i \in \left[d\right], \, j \in \left[m\right].
    \]
    Since \(\sum_{j = 1}^m \widetilde{\*P}_{ij} = 1 - b_i / r_i\) for all \(i \in \left[d\right]\), \(\widetilde{\*P}\) defines a particlewise stochastic projection channel. Let
    \[
    \widetilde{h}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) := g_{\mu}\left(\widetilde{\*P} \boldsymbol{\theta} + \left(1 - \sum_{j = 1}^m \widetilde{\*P}_{ij}\right)_{i \in \left[d\right]}\right) = g_{\mu}\left(\operatorname{diag}\left(\*r\right)^{-1} \left(\*A \boldsymbol{\theta} + \*b\right)\right), \quad \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R^m.
    \]
    Then \(\widetilde{h}\) is the probability-generating function of the output law \(\widetilde{\nu}\) of the particlewise stochastic projection channel associated with \(\widetilde{\*P}\) and input law \(\mu\). Since \(\*r \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\), \(h\) and \(\widetilde{h}\) have the same coefficient support, so \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right) = \operatorname{supp}\left(\widetilde{\nu}\right)\). By \Cref{lem:stochastic-projection-downward-closed-support}, \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\widetilde{\nu}\right)\) is downward closed, and thus so is \(\operatorname{supp}\left(\nu\right)\).

    It remains, by \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization}, to show that \(h\) is strongly log-concave. Let \(\*a_j\) denote the \(j\)-th column of \(\*A\). For every \(\*x \in \mathbb N^m\), the chain rule gives
    \[
    \partial^{\*x} h\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}\right) = \frac{1}{g_{\mu}\left(\*A \*1 + \*b\right)} \left(\partial_{\*a_1}^{x_1} \dots \partial_{\*a_m}^{x_m} g_{\mu}\right)\left(\*A \boldsymbol{\theta} + \*b\right).
    \]
    By the characterization of ULC measures via complete log-concavity in \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization}, \(g_{\mu}\) is completely log-concave. Since \(\*a_1, \dots, \*a_m \in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^d\), \(\partial_{\*a_1}^{x_1} \dots \partial_{\*a_m}^{x_m} g_{\mu}\) is either identically zero or finite, positive, and log-concave on \(\mathbb R_{> 0}^d\). Moreover, \(\*A \boldsymbol{\theta} + \*b \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^d\) for every \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb R_{> 0}^m\), and composition with an affine map preserves log-concavity. Hence \(\partial^{\*x} h\) is either identically zero or finite, positive, and log-concave on \(\mathbb R_{> 0}^m\) for every \(\*x \in \mathbb N^m\). Thus \(h\) is strongly log-concave. Applying \Cref{thm:ulc-generating-function-characterization} once more shows that \(\nu\) is ULC, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
